text:
UN General Assembly resolutions are not a formal source of international law under Article 38 of the ICJ Statute, and they are ordinarily recommendatory rather than binding on member states. Their legal value is mainly as evidence of, or a step toward, customary international law—especially opinio juris—when they command wide support, use normative language, and align with state practice, as the ICJ has treated instruments such as the Friendly Relations Declaration. A narrower set is binding under the Charter itself (budgetary and internal organizational decisions), and many others operate only as soft law that may later harden into custom or treaty rules.

CONFIDENCE: 90
